summary: Defines how a router gets validated route-origin data (which Autonomous System may announce which address block) from a trusted cache that has already checked the RPKI cryptography. Routers stay simple because they never do the heavy certificate checking themselves; they just fetch the results.

plainLanguage.summary: The RPKI-to-Router protocol sends already-validated routing records from a cache to a router. Serial numbers let a router request only changes when it is already up to date.

subtitle: Routers receive validated route-origin data from an RPKI cache.

tldr.problem: Routers need validated information about which Autonomous Systems may announce address prefixes, but the RPKI validation work is assigned to cache systems.
tldr.mechanism: A router connects to a cache and exchanges small binary protocol data units, using session identifiers and serial numbers to request full or incremental updates.
tldr.outcome: The router receives prefix-origin records to use in BGP validation. RFC 8210 later updated this protocol specification.

today: RFC 6810 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013. It has been updated by RFC 8210.

sections.title: Why Routers Use a Cache
sections.content:
Routers use Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) prefix-origin data to check which Autonomous Systems may originate BGP announcements. RFC 6810 defines a protocol for a router to receive this validated data from a trusted cache.

The design separates certificate and object validation from the router. The RFC describes a three-level arrangement: the Global RPKI, local caches that collect and validate its data, and routers that query those caches.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache gathers and checks RPKI data. A router asks the cache for the resulting records instead of validating the source data itself.

sections.title: Cache Sessions and Version Numbers
sections.content:
A router keeps a persistent transport session with one or more configured caches. Each cache has a Session ID for its current instance and a Serial Number for the logical version of its data.

If the router and cache have different Session IDs, they drop the session and the router flushes data learned from that cache. Serial Numbers let a router identify updates only while they belong to the same cache session.
sections.plainLanguage: The session identifier tells the router which cache instance it is talking to. The serial number tells it which version of that cache's records it has received.

sections.title: Protocol Data Units
sections.content:
Each protocol data unit (PDU) begins with an 8-bit protocol version, an 8-bit PDU type, and a 32-bit length that counts the whole PDU. Version 0 is defined here. Unspecified fields are sent as zero.

Routers send Serial Query or Reset Query messages. Caches respond with a Cache Response, zero or more IPv4 or IPv6 prefix records, and End of Data. A prefix record announces or withdraws a prefix and its permitted maximum length for an Autonomous System Number.
sections.plainLanguage: Each short message has a type that says what it does. Prefix messages carry the routing records; other messages request updates, mark their end, or report an error.

sections.title: Full Loads and Incremental Updates
sections.content:
A Reset Query requests the cache's full current data set. A Serial Query asks for records newer than a serial number. The cache sends End of Data with the serial number the router should use after applying the response.

A cache may send Serial Notify as a hint that data changed. A router must still poll at least once an hour. If the cache cannot provide an incremental update, it sends Cache Reset; the router then requests a full load or tries a more preferred cache.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can ask for changes since its last update. If the cache cannot provide them, the router asks for the full set again.

sections.title: Transport and Cache Selection
sections.content:
RFC 6810 requires TCP on port 323 and permits TLS on port 324. It recommends authenticated, integrity-protected transport where available. If unprotected TCP is used, the router and cache MUST share a trusted and controlled network.

A router may be configured with several caches and a preference order. Preference describes proximity, not trust. When changing caches, the router SHOULD retain its old data until it has a full set from another cache.
sections.plainLanguage: A router chooses from its configured cache list. The link matters because the router trusts the cache's records and needs to protect the exchange.

sections.title: Trusting the Cache
sections.content:
The protocol distributes data that a cache has validated, so a router depends on both the cache's identity and the transport. The RFC says mutual authentication and payload integrity are highly desirable, but notes that no protected transport was mandatory to implement across all platforms at publication.

TLS clients present certificates, and routers verify the cache's server certificate. A deployment using unprotected TCP must restrict the connection to a trusted, controlled network.
sections.plainLanguage: The router relies on the cache's records. It must protect the connection or keep it within a trusted network so an attacker cannot impersonate the cache or alter data.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Lowest bit is 1 for announcement and 0 for withdrawal.

fields.name: Autonomous System Number
fields.desc: The Autonomous System allowed to announce the prefix.
